retrieved_context.text: Electrochemical oxidation is generally employed downstream of concentration technologies such as IXR or foam fractionation rather than being applied directly to PFAS- impacted groundwater. This treatment sequence reflects several key constraints at environmentally relevant concen- trations. First, PFAS levels in groundwater typically span the ng L −1 to μg L −1 range, where mass transfer limitations restrict removal efficiency at the electrode surface. Second, the direct application of electrochemical oxidation to groundwater would require prohibitively large electrode areas and high energy input given the large water volumes involved, whereas treatment of concentrated residual streams enables more efficient operation. Third, because PFAS degradation by electrochemical oxidation follows approximately first-order kinetics, higher influent concentrations (mg L −1 ) are associated with reduced specific energy demand compared to μg L −1 influent levels. Finally, the increased solution conductivity of concentrated waste streams alleviates ionic limitations and enhances the effective active area of the reactor, thereby improving overall treatment performance. Key performance metrics for electrochemical oxidation of PFOA include E EO per log removal of PFOA, PFOA removal, and y F . Similar to sensor research, the selectivity of sorbents is crucial but hard to compare as it is greatly impacted by the experimental conditions. Furthermore, few papers of PFAS sorbents demonstrated and discussed the selectivity by comparing the adsorption performance between PFAS and its interferents individually; instead, most of them examined the selectivity as the anti-interferent ability by showing an una ﬀected PFAS adsorption performance in the presence of interferents. This method is not unreasonable in terms of demonstrating the selectivity, but at the same time, one should pay attention to the dosage of sorbents, the species of selected interferents, and the concentrations of all analytes in sample solutions and make sure the una ﬀected performance is not caused by overloading of sorbents or using unrealistic sample solutions. Since the adsorption performance is largely related to the initial concentration of PFAS analyte, all sorbents should be tested under environmentally relevant PFAS concentrations (ng/L to μg/L). However, most existing research conducted adsorption experiments in batch mode under unrealistic initial concentrations (>mg/L), 36,115 which cannot truly re ﬂect the capability of those sorbents in real applications. Furthermore, the performance of more sorbents, especially emerging ones, needs to be tested in the column mode, which is a closer proxy to practical environments.

Two classes of PFAS, perfluoroalkyl car - boxylic acids (PFCAs) and perfluoroalkyl sulfonic acids (PFSAs), are commonly found in legacy stockpiles, in - dustrial waste streams, and as environmental pollutants. Continuous flow supercritical water oxidation (SCWO) reactors have been shown to destroy several PFAS and aqueous film-forming foams. However, a direct com - parison of the SCWO efficacy for PFSAs and PFCAs has not been reported. To address this, this study selected perfluorononanoic acid (PFNA) as a representative compound and employed the ReaxFF reactive force field to simulate its pyrolysis and supercritical water oxidation at the atomic level. In contrast, the SCWO simulation focuses on elucidating its oxidation pathways and product evolution under high temperature, high pressure, and oxygen conditions. Supercritical Water Oxidation SCWO leverages the supercritical phase of water that is achieved by increasing the temperature and pressure of a water- based liquid to a minimum of 374 °C and 218 atm, respectively, as demonstrated in Figure  2. Supercritical water has a relatively high density compared to water vapor at ambient conditions (approximately one- third of the den - sity of liquid water at atmospheric conditions). In this phase, oxygen is fully soluble, resulting in rapid and complete oxi- dation of organics and transforming the feedstock into car - bon dioxide (CO2), water, and inorganic salts, as shown in Figure  3. When SCWO is applied to PFAS, organic fluorine is mineralized to inorganic fluoride. A major advantage of SCWO over other PFAS destruction technologies is its abil- ity to destroy lower molecular weight, shorter chain PFAS compounds (6 carbon chain structures, or C6, and below) in addition to higher molecular weight, legacy PFAS com - pounds (8 carbon chain structures, or C8, and above). PF AS chain length and functional gr oups The physicochemical properties of PFASs, particularly chain length and functional group type, are critical determinants of adsorption behaviour. Long-chain PFASs, such as PFOS and PFOA, tend to exhibit stronger hydrophobic interactions and higher adsorption affinities compared to their short- chain counterparts such as PFBA or PFBS (Vu and Wu 2020). Additionally, sulfonate-functionalised PFASs gener - ally demonstrate higher sorption than carboxylate analogs due to their larger molecular size and stronger electrostatic interactions. Adsorbents must, therefore, be tailored with appropriate surface chemistries or pore architectures to cap - ture both long- and short-chain PFAS species effectively. We used Rapid Small-Scale Column Tests (RSSCTs) to evaluate the performance of a StyDex sorbent and determine the effect of contact time on adsorption of PFAS and pharmaceutical compounds. Contact time is considered an important design parameter for sorption because it is crucial that the contact time is long enough to fully sorb the target contaminants ( Murray et al., 2021 , Pannu et al., 2024 ). Failure to optimize contact time can result in either inefficient removal of target contaminants or unnecessary cost of oper - ation. Therefore, selection of the appropriate contact time is essential for testing and scale-up of novel sorbents ( Murphy et al., 2023 ). The rec - ommended full-scale contact time for removing PFAS by conventional adsorbents is well studied, with a recommended contact time of 2 – 5 min for IX resins and 10 – 30 min for GAC ( Pannu et al., 2024 ). However, the optimal contact time is unknown for novel adsorbents. Therefore, this study focuses on understanding how contact time impacts breakthrough of contaminant mixtures in packed beds of StyDex in wastewater, and the implications for scaling-up to pilot and full-scale operations.
